record.original_question: Can one prove that the fractional part of e^n does not tend to 0 as n tends to infinity?

evidence.quote: We are not yet able to prove that the fractional part of e^n does not tend to 0 as n tends to infinity.

artifact.self_contained_problem: For a real number $x$, let $\{x\} = x - \lfloor x\rfloor \in [0,1)$ denote its fractional part, where $\lfloor x\rfloor$ is the greatest integer not exceeding $x$. Let $e = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 1/k!$ be Euler's number. Prove that the sequence $(\{e^n\})_{n\ge 1}$ does not converge to $0$ as $n \to \infty$; equivalently, show that there exists $\varepsilon > 0$ such that $\{e^n\} > \varepsilon$ for infinitely many positive integers $n$.
artifact.status_search_result: The question of whether the fractional parts of $e^n$ tend to $0$ (or more generally the equidistribution of $\{e^n\}$ mod 1) is widely cited as an open problem. Even basic distributional properties of $\{e^n\}$ and $\{\pi^n\}$ remain unresolved in the literature on equidistribution and dynamics.

status_evidence.title: Open Problems in Dynamics and Related Fields (Gorodnik)
status_evidence.snippet: It is not known whether the sequences (e^n) or (π^n) are equidistributed mod 1.
status_evidence.claim: The distribution mod 1 of e^n is an acknowledged open problem.

status_evidence.title: Equidistributed sequence - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: It is unknown whether the sequences e^n or π^n are equidistributed mod 1.
status_evidence.claim: Behavior of fractional parts of e^n mod 1 is unknown.
